US strike on school in Iran’s Minab was result of over-reliance on AI, outdated SAT images—Bloomberg

Investigation shows that overconfidence in outdated intelligence, imagery and overreliance on artificial intelligence led to the deadliest American military targeting error of the 21st century.

Archishman Ganguly

19 September, 2026 08:29 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

The school damaged in a strike in February in Minab, Iran on 27 August, 2026. Majid Asgaripour/WANA via REUTERS

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: A Pentagon investigation has revealed that a combination of flawed intelligence, outdated satellite (SAT) imagery and an overdependence on artificial intelligence resulted in the US missile strike that killed 123 children at Shajarah Tayyebeh Elementary School in Iran’s Minab on 28 February.

According to a report by Bloomberg , officials directly involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have now said that the strike was caused by what they described as a ‘cascade of preventable failures’. They also identified an array of missed opportunities that could have prevented the tragedy.

The officials, speaking anonymously, revealed that the Trump administration ordered a massive aerial assault on Iran towards the end of February, during which more than 1,000 targets were struck within the first 24 hours. The order squeezed the time frame for finalising targets, sparking an urgency that, compounded with information gaps about the site, staffing cuts in civilian-protection personnel, and an overdependence on AI tech, prepared the ground for the deadly military targeting error.

Show Full Article

Officials part of the internal investigation also emphasised the role of outdated intelligence.

Despite being identified as a military complex years earlier, abundant physical evidence on recent satellite imagery showed that the site had already undergone modifications dating back nearly a decade—construction of walls and entrances separating the school from the military base (2017), and colourfully painted walls adjacent to a football pitch, besides assembly rows and play markings etched on the ground (2018).

However, t he Pentagon, which had characterised the site as a IRGC naval unit base years earlier, failed to upgrade its classification.

In June, The New York Times had also reported that officials overseeing the operation relied on satellite imagery that had not been updated in seven years and did not show a school at the site.

In a separate report in June, Bloomberg had revealed that a US intelligence analyst noticed the changes as early as 2019 and also fed his remarks electronically. But the system was not connected to the primary military intelligence database that aided targeting.

According to officials, artificial intelligence embedded in the Maven Smart System owned by Palantir Technologies Inc., contributed to the disaster since  CENTCOM, which carried out the attack, consisted of personnel over-relying on and over-trusting the AI system.

As 28 February neared, US defence officials were allotted the task of identifying potential targets that would paralyse Iran’s military even before Tehran could respond. The naval division of IRGC was foremost on the list. The site at Minab, erroneously classified as an IRGC facility and fed into Maven, was made a primary target by the software.

All targets usually move through a multi-stage assessment process known in military circles as the ‘kill chain’. Earlier, the process involved intelligence analysts, imagery specialists, targeteers, lawyers, operational commanders and launch crews. However, this time around they were replaced or sidelined by Maven, which condensed several hours of work into a matter of minutes, according to those involved in the Pentagon’s internal review.

The report also points to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s purge of Pentagon’s civilian harm mitigation (CHM) units, which involved slashing headcount across various teams by an overwhelming 90 percent to fewer than 20 staff members. CENTCOM’s strength was, according to the report, reduced from 10 to 1.

A few CENTCOM workers, it added, expected Maven to flag outdated information or incoherencies, but that did not materialise.

(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

Veto, sovereignty & military access—what US and Denmark could get out of Trump’s Greenland deal

Deal could be signed at UNGA next week, according to Danish leadership. Its signing could bring to an end saga between the US and the rest of NATO over the fate of the island.

Keshav Padmanabhan

19 September, 2026 06:51 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational | A drone view shows houses on the shore of Nuuk, Greenland, on 7 February, 2026 | Stoyan Nenov/Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US President Donald J. Trump’s Friday announcement, of an agreement with Denmark over Greenland, comes after months of high-stakes negotiations over an island that the American President has sought to purchase during the course of his two presidencies.

The announcement made by Trump is light on details of the full contours of the deal, but highlights key points of what Washington considers a part of the deal.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has welcomed the agreement as “great for NATO [North Atlantic Treaty Organisation] and Europe as well”.

Show Full Article

Trump’s deal for greater military access in Greenland falls short of his call for handing over the territory to the US, an outcome he had deemed as “unacceptable” in January. The new agreement, according to Trump, will ensure “permanent US control” over security of the self-governing autonomous territory part of the Kingdom of Denmark, while also underlining that “no adversary” will ever build a base on the island.

The agreement is likely to be signed next week on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), potentially easing transatlantic tensions.

Trump and the other NATO member-states, including Denmark, have had major differences over the fate of Greenland, especially as the US President called for either annexation or the purchase of the island during the early months of his second term.

ThePrint explains the contours of the deal as it currently stands.

Also Read: ‘Will not take Greenland by force…we will remember if Europe says no,’ Trump says at Davos

‘Permanent control’ over security of Greenland The agreement is expected to allow greater American military presence in Greenland, while preventing China or Russia from stationing troops or building bases in the strategically placed Arctic island, according to Bloomberg .

The US will be empowered to restrict investments in Greenland made by countries it deems as adversaries, reports Bloomberg , while also allowing Washington to act to safeguard its interests in the region.

The island found to the Northeast of Canada is roughly 2.16 million square kilometres in size, with over 39,000 kilometres of coastline. Around 80 percent of the island is covered by a large ice-sheet, which is the second largest in the world, following Antarctica.

The strategic importance of Greenland has grown in recent decades, especially with record rates of melting ice across the Arctic, which has led to more activities by countries in the region.

Russia is one of the eight countries to have a geographical footprint in the Arctic, alongside Canada, Norway, Finland, Denmark, Iceland, Sweden and the US.

Other countries including China and India have also shown interest in the Arctic for multiple reasons. From research into the melting ice-caps for better understanding of glacial melt in the Himalayas, to the Northern Sea Route, the region has increasingly become important for countries outside its immediate vicinity.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many. We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction,” Trump said in a statement on the micro-blogging platform X.

The latest agreement could potentially allow the US a potential veto over any investments in Greenland from countries like Russia and China, given American concerns that Chinese or Russian investment, especially in sensitive areas such as minerals, could impact the US’ position in Greenland.

The US in Greenland since WWII The US’ interest in Greenland is not new. Since World War II, its military has had a presence in Greenland. The American military moved quickly to capture the island during WWII, after NAZI Germany occupied Denmark in the summer of 1940.

Denmark and the US eventually negotiated a military treaty in 1951, which allowed the US the right to build military bases across Greenland as long as prior consent was sought from Copenhagen.

The US will likely not require any consent from Denmark or Greenland to expand its military footprint on the island, according to the BBC . Throughout the Cold War, the US maintained a number of military installations in Greenland, especially as the polar route was the quickest trajectory for an inter-continental ballistic missile between the US and the Soviet Union.

The US eventually reduced the number of its active bases to just one at Thule, which was renamed as the Pituffik Space Base in 2023. The US-Denmark 1951 agreement has been amended and supplemented in the past, including in 2004 signed in Igaliku between the two countries. The primary fixture in all these agreements remained the Danish consent required for US military presence.

The agreement, which could be signed next week on the margins of the UNGA, may finally bring to an end the ongoing chapter between the US and the rest of NATO over the fate of Greenland. Trump’s provocative claims, including over the territory, had led to an united response by Europe, which inflamed tensions within the transatlantic partnership.

Frederiksen’s response to the agreement highlights that the deal recognises Denmark’s sovereignty over the Arctic island. Greenland also welcomed the agreement, while making no comment on the final contours of the deal.

(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

20-hour standoff in Pakistan’s Kohat began with car bombing, ends with killing of 8 militants

Provincial police chief confirms that the attack involved a suicide bomber. The complex houses district-level police headquarters and units including Counter Terrorism Dept.

Debdutta Chakraborty

19 September, 2026 04:39 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

People gather at a damaged mosque following a suicide attack at a police facility in Kohat, Pakistan | Reuters/Stringer

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Eight militants were killed by Pakistani forces after a 20-hour standoff in Kohat district, marking an end of the operation that began Friday after twin strikes at a police compound in the restive northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province.

The toll stood at 31, including 16 policemen, and more than 100 injured in the attack whose responsibility was claimed by the Hafiz Gul Bahadur-led Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen.

The standoff was preceded by a suicide car bombing and gun assault at a mosque inside the Old Police Lines complex in Kohat, a city in KP province, near the Afghanistan border.

Show Full Article

An explosives-laden vehicle rammed into the entrance of the police compound as worshippers gathered for prayers at the mosque. The militants, according to local reports, then engaged in a gun battle with security forces and KP police.

The complex houses district-level police headquarters as well as units including the Counter Terrorism Department and Special Branch. The assault came a day after a roadside bomb struck a security-forces convoy in neighbouring Hangu district, killing six soldiers.

Provincial police chief Zulfikar Hameed confirmed that the attack involved a suicide bomber. After the initial explosion, armed militants attempted to enter the police compound and engaged officers in a prolonged exchange of gunfire, he told Reuters.

On Saturday, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa posted that the operation ended with the elimination of eight militants.

Following the blast at the Old Police Lines Mosque in Kohat, terrorists attempted to infiltrate; 8 terrorists were killed in retaliatory action by police and security forces.

IG KP Zulfiqar Hameed lauded the officers who took part in the operation and announced rewards. pic.twitter.com/OYvB81LjyF

— KP Police (@KP_Police1) September 19, 2026

In 2010, the police complex had suffered the brunt of a similar suicide car bombing which had then claimed at least 20 lives. Lashkar-e-Jhangvi, another anti-Shia Deobandi group, had claimed responsibility for the attack.

Also Read: Pakistan signs interceptor drone deal with Trump family-backed Powerus

What is Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan? In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), or the Pakistani Taliban, remains the militant group operating along the Afghan-Pakistan border.

But competing factions and alliances have increasingly challenged its position. The Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, or IMP, comprises the Hafiz Gul Bahadur Group, or HGBG; Harakat Inqilab-e-Islami Pakistan, or HIIP; and Lashkar-e-Islam, or LeI.

Since its formation in April 2025, IMP has evolved into a militant umbrella alliance rather than functioning as a single, distinct organisation. The alliance has been particularly active in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. HGBG, the faction associated with Hafiz Gul Bahadur, is regarded as the most experienced and dominant component of the coalition.

A Deobandi militant faction based in North Waziristan and nearby areas of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the HGBG is led by Pashtun leader Hafiz Gul Bahadur, who is affiliated with the Afghan Taliban and the Haqqani Network. Estimates put its size at roughly 1,000 to 1,500 fighters.

Bahadur was named the first deputy head of the TTP when it came into being in December 2007. Infighting followed because he insisted on attacking targets in Afghanistan, rather than the Pakistani government. As his group maintained ties with the Pakistani government, media and officials dubbed it the “good Taliban”. A 2009 analysis called Bahadur ‘the survivalist of North Waziristan’.

That peace arrangement ended in 2014, when Pakistan launched Operation Zarb-e-Azb against all militants in North Waziristan, including those of HGB. Bahadur then fully aligned with jihadist elements and relocated to Afghanistan. After the Taliban took over Afghanistan in 2021, HGB shifted its activities against Pakistan and collaborated further with other militant groups.

The Pakistan army claims the group operates from Afghanistan. The Inter-Services Public Relations, the media and public relations wing of the Pakistan armed forces, had blamed the July 2024 Bannu Cantonment attack on it following which Pakistan’s National Counter Terrorism Authority formally designated the group a terrorist organisation in July 2024.

In 2025, Bahadur was reported to be the leader of a new alliance, Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, which carried out ambushes and rocket and grenade attacks in North Waziristan and Tirah.

It reportedly used anti-drone technology together with the TTP. In July that year, IMP claimed that it carried out more than 90 attacks against security forces across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Reports indicated that June 2025 had brought a sharp increase in militant attacks and counterterrorism operations.

While some describe HGB as affiliated with or aligned with the TTP, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies emphasizes that the faction maintains an independent command structure and follows its own agenda.

HGB is rooted largely among the Wazir and Dawar tribes of North Waziristan. TTP has historically been dominated by the Mehsud tribal network of South Waziristan. The two groups have consequently been involved in competition over resources, authority and territorial control.

In a paper, Safdar Sial, an expert at the Pakistan Institute for Peace Studies, has described HGB as a growing security threat as it carried out large numbers of attacks against Pakistani forces. The violence in Kohat is part of a broader deterioration in security along Pakistan’s western frontier, according to Sial.

Islamabad has repeatedly accused groups like TTP of using safe havens in Afghanistan to train, organise and plan attacks inside Pakistan. The Taliban government has rejected those accusations, saying that militancy inside Pakistan is a domestic problem.

The dispute has contributed to growing tensions between the two neighbours, which have exchanged cross-border strikes intermittently.

Kohat occupies a strategic position in this region. The city is close to the Afghan border and serves as a major route toward North Waziristan, as well as toward Bannu and Dera Ismail Khan, areas that have experienced repeated militant attacks in recent months.

The district’s population is overwhelmingly Pashtun. According to the 2023 census, Pashto is the dominant mother tongue of more than 85 percent of Kohat District’s residents.

The Kohat terrorist incident, according to Pakistan’s former Special representative to Afghanistan Asif Durrani, again exposes the erosion of the state’s writ in parts of Pakistan.

“Counterterrorism is not merely about force; it requires winning the confidence, cooperation and support of the people. In KP and Balochistan, that vital element appears increasingly weak,” Durrani posted on X.

“This delicate moment once again calls for serious introspection. A more coordinated socio-political response designed to reinforce the state’s narrative is vital for a winning proposition. Pakistan will not be the last to bleed if the Taliban continue to have their way,” Express Tribune wrote in an editorial Saturday.

(Edited by Tony Rai)
